content:
On Sunday, wildfires continued to ravage multiple areas in the western United States and Canada, with some residents closely monitoring possible evacuation orders while others, already forced to flee their homes, waited to see what remained when they could return.

In western Canada, more than 20,000 people were forced to evacuate over the weekend from communities along Okanagan Lake in British Columbia as fast-spreading wildfires destroyed homes and dozens had to be rescued by aircraft. In the United States, three wildfires in the Spokane area of Washington state have been burning for over a week, with firefighters continuing to conduct mop-up work near the containment lines.

Laurie Allen evacuated the Nine Mile Falls community north of Spokane last weekend with her husband, dog and two kittens, as a wildfire burned a short distance away. The road to her home remained closed on Sunday, but she said she had heard from friends that, although covered in ash, her house and nearby homes were still intact.

"I've lived here for 65 years and have never seen anything like this," Allen said. "We were just thinking about getting the animals out and leaving. But now it's affecting so many friends and family around us, so it's really heartbreaking."

Over 20,000 evacuated due to Canada wildfires

In Canada, Anette Boulet was among those evacuated from Summerland, a community of about 12,000 on the shores of Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. She and her family evacuated around 4:30 a.m. on Saturday, when their home was already enveloped in thick smoke.

"You could barely see anything, it was dark, and flames were coming at you from the ridge," Boulet said. She subsequently moved to an evacuation centre in Penticton.

"It's indescribable," she said. "That feeling of fear."

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said later on Sunday that an 80-year-old woman had died while attempting to flee the Okanagan Lake area wildfires.

In addition to the evacuations in Summerland, the Bald Range wildfire—first reported Friday evening—also led to the evacuation of about 8,000 people in the nearby area of Peachland. British Columbia declared a state of emergency on Saturday.

Eleanor Olszewski, Canada's Minister of Emergency Management and Community Resilience, said on social media on Sunday that she had approved a request for federal assistance to British Columbia to provide shelter and accommodation for those forced to evacuate.

Spokane area wildfires keep residents on edge

The teams managing the three wildfires in the Spokane area issued a news release on Sunday saying that firefighters were continuing to conduct "mop-up work" near the containment lines, and none of the three fires had continued to spread. Over the past week, the fires have destroyed or damaged approximately 920 structures.

Earlier in the week, a man was arrested and charged with intentionally starting the largest of the three Spokane-area wildfires.

Residents of Malden, a remote town about 35 miles (55 kilometres) south of Spokane, were urged to evacuate immediately on Saturday. However, by Sunday the evacuation level had been downgraded, with residents only needing to be prepared to evacuate quickly if necessary.

"The winds are fairly calm and the fire isn't spreading," said John Goyke, whose company contracts to operate the water supply for Malden. "But we are keeping in touch with everyone via social media and Facebook."

Goyke is also the mayor of neighbouring Rosalia. He said Malden residents had been told to conserve water so that it could be reserved for fire trucks if needed, and that the Malden fire department had been hauling water in from Rosalia.

In 2020, most of Malden was destroyed in a wildfire, including the fire station, post office, town hall and library.

Two firefighters killed in helicopter crash

In Utah, two helicopter pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed while fighting a fire in the Fishlake National Forest on Friday morning. Rescue crews finally reached the scene on Saturday and confirmed both had died.

Officials said on Sunday that steep, rugged terrain, combined with active wildfire, had prevented them from reaching the scene quickly.

Sevier County Sheriff Nathan Curtis said: "When we first arrived, we saw two separate columns of smoke—one from the crash site and one from an active fire that was coming toward us."

The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the cause of the crash.

___

Associated Press reporter Holly Ramer contributed to this report.
